questions.stem: Palisade mesophyll cells are tightly packed near the upper epidermis. How is this arrangement an adaptation for photosynthesis?

options.text: It prevents water loss from the leaf
It positions cells with the most chloroplasts closest to the light source for maximum light absorption
It allows gases to diffuse more slowly
It provides structural support for the leaf

questions.explanation: Palisade cells contain the most chloroplasts of any leaf cell type and are positioned near the upper surface where light intensity is greatest. Their elongated, tightly packed arrangement ensures maximum light absorption. Light intensity decreases as it passes through cell layers, so having these cells at the top is the most efficient arrangement.

questions.stem: The spongy mesophyll has large air spaces between its cells. What is the primary function of these air spaces?

options.text: To make the leaf lighter so it can face the sun
To allow gases (CO2 and O2) to diffuse easily through the leaf to and from the photosynthesising cells
To store water for dry periods
To insulate the leaf against cold temperatures

questions.explanation: The air spaces in the spongy mesophyll provide a large internal surface area and pathways for gas exchange. CO2 from the air enters through stomata and diffuses through these spaces to reach the palisade cells for photosynthesis. Oxygen produced during photosynthesis also diffuses out through these spaces.

questions.stem: Guard cells can open and close stomata. On a hot, dry day, what would you expect the stomata to do, and why?

options.text: Open wide to increase cooling by releasing more heat
Close to reduce water loss through transpiration, even though this limits CO2 uptake
Remain open because photosynthesis needs to continue
Close because no gas exchange is needed on hot days

questions.explanation: On hot, dry days, the rate of transpiration (water loss) is very high. To prevent excessive water loss that could cause wilting, guard cells lose water, become flaccid, and the stomata close. This is a trade-off -- closing stomata conserves water but also reduces CO2 uptake, slowing photosynthesis.

questions.stem: The upper epidermis of a leaf is covered by a waxy cuticle. A student suggests removing the cuticle would improve photosynthesis. Why is this suggestion incorrect?

options.text: The cuticle is transparent, so it does not block light significantly, but it does prevent water loss
The cuticle provides all the light for photosynthesis
The cuticle is where photosynthesis takes place
The cuticle absorbs CO2 for the leaf

questions.explanation: The waxy cuticle is largely transparent, allowing light to pass through to the photosynthetic cells below. Its primary function is preventing water loss from the leaf surface. Removing it would cause the plant to lose water rapidly through evaporation, leading to wilting and potentially death, without significantly increasing light availability for photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Xylem and phloem run through the veins of a leaf. Which statement correctly describes their roles in the leaf?

options.text: Xylem carries glucose away; phloem brings water in
Xylem brings water and minerals to the leaf; phloem carries sugars away from the leaf
Both carry water to the leaf
Xylem carries CO2 to the leaf; phloem carries O2 away

questions.explanation: Xylem vessels transport water and dissolved minerals from the roots to the leaf (needed for photosynthesis and to replace water lost through transpiration). Phloem tubes transport dissolved sugars (mainly sucrose) from the leaf (where they are made by photosynthesis) to the rest of the plant for use or storage. This is called translocation.
